newsitem.title: UK: Copper drops in sell-off after rally above $2,000 a tonne.
newsitem.headline: Copper drops in sell-off after rally above $2,000 a tonne.

text.p: The world price of copper dropped almost $100 a tonne on Tuesday in a sudden sell-off after it had seemed set on making a rally.

News of a big decline in copper stocks failed to bring in enough buying to overcome selling at the higher prices. And the extent of selling led some traders to speculate that banks may still be unwinding a hoard of copper built up by Sumitomo Corp of Japan.

The market then took a dive. Copper had hit a high at $2,042 on Monday but eased later to end the day at $2,016. In Tuesday's fall it went as low as $1,916 before edging up to around $1,930 in late activity.
The metal had seemed poised last week to shake off the blues that have prevailed since the disgrace back in June of the Japanese mastermind of a high price copper trading strategy, Yasuo Hamanaka.

Behind the attempt at a rally was a drop in world stocks of copper that have fallen 60 percent since last year. A new fall in LME-supervised warehouse stocks was reported on Tuesday of 13,475 tonnes to a six-year low of 132,350 tonnes.
The failure to react to that stock figure suggested to some traders that long positions originally belonging to Japan's Sumitomo Corp were still being sold in to rallies.
"To me it's a miracle this market isn't any higher. Some positions must still be around from the Sumitomo scandal," a senior trader said.

Some also heard that influential Montreal scrap metal dealer Herbie Black might be selling copper again. His sales last June contributed to a price rout in a market unerved by rumours, later confirmed, that Hamanaka was in trouble.
Aluminium eased with flagship copper on Tuesday to end the London afternoon at $1,408 per tonne.
Elsewhere on commodity markets, Chicago wheat futures were again just easier slightly below $3.85 per bushel for December.
Crude oil prices fell under pressure from speculators who suspected that a recent "bull run" might be ending.
They thought that U.S. stock data due after trading ends on Tuesday might show a long-awaited build in heating oil stocks ahead of the northern hemisphere winter.
The December contract for benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea was down some 75 cents in the London afternoon at around $23.75 a barrel compared with 24 hours prevously.
The precious metals also lost further value on Tuesday after prices were chased lower by trade selling shortly after the New York markets opened, dealers said.
"The whole sector is looking relatively sickly but whether it's weak enough to go lower we'll have to see," a dealer said.
Silver led the way down. Speculative selling triggered sell orders from computer-controlled investment programmes.
Gold was fixed in London at $381.70 per ounce on Tuesday. Silver fell eight cents from Monday's London close to a setting at $4.85 an ounce.
Coffee firmed in thin mostly technical trading and cocoa recovered slightly after skidding on Monday. Sugar eased in a thin market with no news to give direction.
